title: Can You Refer a Client to an Out-of-State Real Estate Agent?
metaDesc: Can a Florida-licensed referral agent send a client to an agent in another state? Yes, here's how out-of-state real estate referrals actually work.
h1: Can You Refer a Client to an Out-of-State Real Estate Agent?
about: Whether a Florida referral agent can send a client to a licensed agent in another state
answer: Yes. A Florida-licensed referral agent can refer a client to a licensed agent in any other state, not just Florida. The referral fee agreement is still between the two brokerages, and the fee is only payable to a properly licensed agent or brokerage in that state.
takeaways: Florida referral agents aren't limited to sending clients to Florida agents; any state works.
The receiving agent must hold an active license in whatever state the property is located in.
The referral agreement and fee still flow broker to broker, the same as an in-state referral.
This matters most for clients relocating away from Florida, or Florida buyers looking elsewhere.
Confirm the receiving brokerage's license status before sending a referral out of state.
tldr: Yes, a Florida referral agent can send a client to a licensed agent anywhere in the country, not only Florida. The same rules apply: a written broker-to-broker agreement, and the fee only goes to a properly licensed real estate professional in that state.
body:
Can I refer a client outside of Florida?

Yes. There’s nothing that limits a Florida-licensed referral agent to sending clients only to other Florida agents. If your client is moving to Georgia, the Carolinas, or anywhere else, you can refer them to a properly licensed agent in that state and still earn a referral fee.

Does the process work any differently?

Not really. The same basic rule applies wherever the property is: the referral fee can only be paid to a licensed real estate professional, active in that state, and the agreement is still made broker to broker rather than agent to agent. It’s worth confirming the receiving brokerage’s license status before making the introduction, just as you would locally.

When does this come up most often?

Two common situations: a Florida client who’s relocating out of state for work, family, or retirement, and a client from another state who mentions they’re moving to Florida. Either direction, the referral works the same way, and it’s often the easiest, most valuable kind of referral, since you likely can’t serve that market yourself even if you were still actively selling.

How do you find a licensed agent in another state to refer to?

Often through the brokerage holding your license, since many referral networks have relationships with agents and brokerages well beyond their own state. If your brokerage doesn’t have an existing contact where your client is headed, a quick license lookup with that state’s real estate regulator confirms who’s properly licensed before you make the introduction.

Referral requirements can vary by state; confirm current rules with the receiving brokerage and, where needed, that state's licensing authority. Educational only, not legal advice.

faq.q: Can a Florida real estate referral agent refer a client to another state?
faq.a: Yes. A Florida-licensed referral agent can refer a client to a properly licensed agent in any other state, not only Florida.

faq.q: Does an out-of-state referral fee agreement work differently?
faq.a: Not really. It still requires a written agreement between the two brokerages and the fee can only be paid to a licensed real estate professional active in that state.

faq.q: What's the most common reason for an out-of-state referral?
faq.a: A client relocating away from Florida for work, family, or retirement, or a client from elsewhere who mentions they're moving to Florida. Either direction works the same way.

ctaHeading: Your network isn't limited to Florida.
